blocks.text: A mains socket is labelled 230 V, but an oscilloscope shows the voltage peaking at about 325 V, and a vibration sensor on a pump shows a current that lags that voltage by a fraction of a millisecond. Which of those numbers is 'the' voltage, and how do you add two waveforms that are shifted in time? Phasors give a precise answer to both.

blocks.markdown: A **sinusoid** is the signal $v(t)=V_p\cos(\omega t+\theta)$ (or with $\sin$). Its **amplitude** or peak value is $V_p$ (volts); its **angular frequency** is $\omega=2\pi f$ in rad/s, where $f$ is the frequency in hertz and the period is $T=1/f$; and its **phase** $\theta$ (degrees or radians) says where in its cycle it starts at $t=0$. A sinusoid is completely fixed by $V_p$, $\omega$ and $\theta$.

blocks.title: RMS value
blocks.text: The root-mean-square value of a periodic signal is $V_{rms}=\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$, the DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sinusoid, $\overline{\cos^2}=\tfrac12$, so $V_{rms}=V_p/\sqrt2\approx0.707\,V_p$.

blocks.caption: Relations for a sinusoid; Vpp is the peak-to-peak voltage

blocks.markdown: **Phasors.** In a linear circuit driven at a single frequency $\omega$, every voltage and current is a sinusoid at that same $\omega$. Only amplitude and phase differ, so we drop the common $\omega t$ and keep a complex number, the **phasor**: $\mathbf V=V\angle\theta$. By convention we use the cosine as the reference: $v(t)=V_p\cos(\omega t+\theta)\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf V=V_p\angle\theta$. Phasors may be written with peak or rms magnitude; state which you use (power calculations favour rms). A sine is converted to cosine with $\sin(\omega t+\theta)=\cos(\omega t+\theta-90^\circ)$.

blocks.title: From waveform to phasor
blocks.prompt: A mains voltage is $v(t)=311\cos(314t+30^\circ)$ V. Find the frequency, period, rms value and the rms phasor.

steps.text: Write the phasor in polar form, with a cosine reference.

blocks.answer: 50 Hz, period 20 ms, 220 V rms, phasor 220 angle 30 degrees (rectangular 190.5 + j110 V).

blocks.markdown: **Phase difference.** For two sinusoids of the same frequency, $v=V_p\cos(\omega t+\theta_v)$ and $i=I_p\cos(\omega t+\theta_i)$, the phase difference is $\varphi=\theta_v-\theta_i$. If $\varphi>0$ the voltage **leads** the current (its peaks come earlier); if $\varphi<0$ it lags. A time shift $\Delta t$ between peaks corresponds to a phase $\varphi=360^\circ\,f\,\Delta t$. Phase is meaningful only between waveforms of the same frequency.

blocks.title: Phase difference of a voltage and current
blocks.prompt: A load has $v=12\sin(\omega t+20^\circ)$ V and $i=0.40\sin(\omega t-25^\circ)$ A. Convert both to cosine-reference phasors and find the phase difference.

steps.text: Convert $\sin$ to $\cos$ by subtracting $90^\circ$ from each phase.

blocks.answer: The voltage leads the current by 45 degrees. The same difference results if both are left in sine form, since the 90 degree offset cancels.

items: Compare phases only at the same frequency, and use the same trig function (cosine) as reference.
Always state whether a phasor magnitude is peak or rms.
Adding sinusoids of the same frequency is done by adding phasors (as complex numbers).

blocks.title: Sine versus cosine
blocks.text: Mixing sine and cosine forms is the commonest phasor error. $10\sin(\omega t)$ has phasor $10\angle-90^\circ$ in the cosine reference, not $10\angle0^\circ$.

points: A phasor $V\angle\theta$ represents $V\cos(\omega t+\theta)$; convert sines using $\sin=\cos(\cdot-90^\circ)$.
Phase difference $\varphi=\theta_v-\theta_i$; positive means voltage leads. A time shift gives $\varphi=360^\circ f\Delta t$.

questions.stem: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak value of 170 V. What is its rms value?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the peak value.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this multiplies by sqrt(2) instead of dividing.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this halves the peak, which would be the average over a half-cycle approximation misused.

questions.explanation: RMS is peak divided by $\sqrt2$: $170/1.414=120.2$ V. Multiplying by $\sqrt2$ would convert rms back to peak.

questions.stem: A sinusoidal supply is 24 V rms. What is its peak voltage?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this divides by sqrt(2) instead of multiplying.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the peak-to-peak value doubled from rms, which is incorrect.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the rms value itself.

questions.stem: Using peak magnitudes and a cosine reference, what is the phasor of $v(t)=10\cos(\omega t+60^\circ)$ V?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: amplitude 10 V and phase +60 degrees.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the sign of the phase is wrong.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: 7.07 V would be the rms magnitude, but the question asks for peak.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this adds 90 degrees, as if converting to a sine.

questions.explanation: A cosine reference means the phasor is just $V_p\angle\theta$ with $V_p=10$ V and $\theta=+60^\circ$.

questions.stem: $v=15\cos(\omega t+10^\circ)$ V and $i=3\cos(\omega t-50^\circ)$ A. What is the phase relationship?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: sign reversed; positive phase difference means lead.

questions.explanation: The phase difference is $\theta_v-\theta_i=10^\circ-(-50^\circ)=+60^\circ$, so the voltage leads the current by 60 degrees.

questions.stem: What is the phasor (cosine reference, peak magnitude) of $v(t)=8\sin(\omega t+40^\circ)$ V?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sin(x) = cos(x - 90), so the phase is 40 - 90 = -50 degrees.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this treats the sine as a cosine.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this adds 90 degrees instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Convert to cosine form: $8\sin(\omega t+40^\circ)=8\cos(\omega t+40^\circ-90^\circ)=8\cos(\omega t-50^\circ)$, giving $8\angle-50^\circ$ V.

questions.stem: A sinusoidal current measured on an oscilloscope has a peak-to-peak value of 6.0 A. What is its rms value in amperes?
questions.explanation: The peak value is half the peak-to-peak: $I_p=3.0$ A. Then $I_{rms}=3.0/\sqrt2=2.12$ A. A common mistake is to divide the peak-to-peak value directly.

questions.stem: A 400 Hz voltage peak occurs 0.30 ms before the corresponding current peak. What is the phase angle by which the voltage leads the current, in degrees?
questions.explanation: One cycle takes $T=2.5$ ms, which is $360^\circ$. A 0.30 ms shift is $360\times0.30/2.5=43.2^\circ$, equivalently $360^\circ fT$ with $f=400$ Hz.

questions.stem: Two voltages of the same frequency are $v_1=6\cos\omega t$ V and $v_2=8\sin\omega t$ V. Using phasors, find the amplitude (peak value) of the sum $v_1+v_2$, in volts.
questions.explanation: In the cosine reference, $v_1\to6\angle0^\circ=6$ and $v_2\to8\angle-90^\circ=-j8$. The sum is $6-j8$ with magnitude $\sqrt{36+64}=10$ V and phase $-53.1^\circ$.

questions.stem: Explain what the rms value of a sinusoidal voltage means physically, and show why it equals the peak value divided by $\sqrt2$.
markingGuide: RMS is the equivalent DC value that delivers the same average power to a resistor
Power is proportional to v^2, so take the mean of the square
Mean of cos^2 over a cycle equals 1/2
Therefore V_rms^2 = V_p^2/2 and V_rms = V_p/sqrt(2)
questions.explanation: RMS is defined so that a resistor dissipates the same average power as from a DC source of that voltage. Since power is $v^2/R$, we need the mean of $v^2$: $\overline{V_p^2\cos^2\omega t}=V_p^2/2$ because the average of $\cos^2$ over a cycle is $1/2$. Taking the square root gives $V_{rms}=V_p/\sqrt2\approx0.707V_p$.

questions.stem: A load has $v=20\sin(100t+30^\circ)$ V and $i=2.0\sin(100t-15^\circ)$ A. Find the frequency, write both as rms phasors (cosine reference) and state the phase difference and which signal leads.
markingGuide: omega = 100 rad/s so f = 100/(2 pi) = 15.9 Hz
Converts sine to cosine: V phase = 30 - 90 = -60 degrees, I phase = -15 - 90 = -105 degrees
Phasors 14.14 angle -60 degrees V and 1.414 angle -105 degrees A
Phase difference = -60 - (-105) = +45 degrees: voltage leads current
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is $100$ rad/s, so $f=100/2\pi=15.9$ Hz. In the cosine reference, $\mathbf V=(20/\sqrt2)\angle(30-90)^\circ=14.14\angle-60^\circ$ V and $\mathbf I=(2.0/\sqrt2)\angle(-15-90)^\circ=1.414\angle-105^\circ$ A. The phase difference is $-60-(-105)=+45^\circ$, so the voltage leads the current by $45^\circ$.
